systems.name: Brain, sleep and mood
systems.about: Sleep and mood are the first things to slip under isolation, confinement and a shifted day-night cycle, and they drag everything else down with them.

systems.name: Heart and circulation
systems.about: Without gravity, blood and fluid move towards the head and the heart works against less load. Heart rate and blood pressure show how the circulation is adapting.

systems.name: Lungs and oxygen
systems.about: A closed cabin can build up carbon dioxide and its air is all you have. Blood oxygen is the quick check.

systems.name: Blood sugar and energy
systems.about: Spaceflight changes how the body handles sugar. Diet, stress, poor sleep and less muscle use all push it.

systems.name: Body temperature
systems.about: Body heat is harder to shed without convection, and fever is the first sign of infection in a crew that cannot leave.

systems.name: Kidneys, fluids and salts
systems.about: Fluid shifts and low water intake raise the risk of dehydration and kidney stones. The kidneys also keep the blood's salts in balance.

systems.name: Liver
systems.about: The liver processes nutrients and medication. Its enzymes in the blood show strain.

systems.name: Bones
systems.about: Weight-bearing bones lose about 1% to 1.5% of their mineral density per month in microgravity unless they are loaded by exercise.

systems.name: Muscle and body mass
systems.about: Muscles that no longer carry your weight shrink quickly. Body mass and exercise time track it.

indicators.name: Resting heart rate
indicators.how: Sit still for five minutes, strapped in or holding a handrail. Use the pulse oximeter or count the pulse at your wrist for 60 seconds. Measure at the same time each day, before exercise and caffeine.
indicators.why: Resting heart rate rises with dehydration, infection, poor sleep, stress and deconditioning. A steady climb over days is an early warning.
sources: Adult resting range 60-100 bpm (American Heart Association); trained adults are often lower, so the lower watch level here is 50

high: Re-measure after five minutes of complete rest.
Drink 250-500 mL of water and check your hydration reading.
Check your temperature: a fast pulse with fever suggests infection.
Skip caffeine and hard exercise until it settles.
low: Re-measure. A low pulse in a fit person at rest is often normal.
Note any dizziness, fainting or chest discomfort; with any of these, treat this as urgent.
shift: Your resting pulse has moved away from your own normal. Look at sleep, hydration and temperature over the same days.

indicators.name: Blood pressure, upper (systolic)
indicators.how: Rest for five minutes. Put the cuff on your bare upper arm at heart level, keep still and silent, and take two readings one minute apart. Enter the second.
indicators.why: Fluid moves towards the head in microgravity and the circulation resets. Pressure that climbs, or falls with dizziness, needs attention before a spacewalk or landing.
sources: American Heart Association categories: normal below 120/80, elevated 120-129, stage 1 130-139 or 80-89, stage 2 from 140 or 90, crisis above 180 and/or 120

high: Re-measure after five quiet minutes, cuff at heart level.
Cut back on salty food today and drink water.
Note headache, vision change, chest pain or shortness of breath; any of these with a high reading is urgent.
low: Re-measure. Drink water and take in some salt with food.
Move slowly when changing posture or starting exercise.
Dizziness or fainting with a low reading should be reported.
shift: Your pressure has moved away from your own normal. Compare with body mass and hydration: both follow fluid balance.

indicators.name: Blood pressure, lower (diastolic)
indicators.how: This is the second number from the same cuff reading.
indicators.why: The lower number is the pressure between heartbeats. It is read together with the upper number.
sources: American Heart Association categories (see upper number)

high: Re-measure after five quiet minutes.
Cut back on salty food today and drink water.
low: Re-measure. Drink water and move slowly when changing posture.
shift: Your lower pressure has moved away from your own normal.

indicators.name: Blood sugar, fasting
indicators.how: Measure before breakfast, at least eight hours after eating. Wash and dry your hands, prick the side of a fingertip, wipe away the first drop and apply the second to the strip. In microgravity the drop stays on the finger: bring the strip to the drop.
indicators.why: Blood sugar control weakens in spaceflight. In the Inspiration4 crew it rose 14% to 44% above each person's own pre-flight level after a three-day flight.
sources: American Diabetes Association: fasting normal below 100 mg/dL, 100-125 raised, 126 or more high; low below 70, clinically significant low below 54

high: Confirm it was a fasting reading; re-measure tomorrow before eating.
Favour protein and fibre over sugary items for the next meals.
Do your exercise session: working muscle takes up sugar.
Protect tonight's sleep; short sleep raises morning sugar.
low: Re-measure now with a new strip and clean, dry hands.
If it is still low, or you feel shaky, sweaty or confused, take 15 g of fast sugar (juice or glucose tablets) and re-measure after 15 minutes.
Do not exercise or start a critical task until it is back above 70.
shift: Your fasting sugar has moved away from your own normal even though it is inside the textbook range. This is the pattern seen after spaceflight; keep measuring daily.

indicators.name: Body temperature
indicators.how: Use the same thermometer and the same site every time (ear or under the tongue). Wait 30 minutes after exercise, food or drink.
indicators.why: Infection in a sealed cabin spreads to the whole crew, and the immune system is weaker in flight. Fever is the earliest objective sign.
sources: Fever commonly defined as 38.0 °C or above; normal adult range roughly 36.1-37.2 °C

high: Re-measure in 30 minutes at rest.
Rest, drink fluids and check the cabin temperature and your clothing.
Note other symptoms: cough, sore throat, pain, rash, stomach upset.
Keep your distance from crewmates and wear a mask until it is clear whether this is an infection.
low: Re-measure. Warm up with clothing and a warm drink, then check again.
shift: Your temperature has moved away from your own normal. Watch it over the next readings.

indicators.name: Blood oxygen
indicators.how: Warm your hand, clip the pulse oximeter on a finger without nail polish, keep still and read it after the number has been steady for ten seconds.
indicators.why: Oxygen saturation falls when the cabin air is off (low oxygen or high carbon dioxide) or the lungs are affected. It is the fastest check you have.
sources: Normal 95-100%; below about 92% generally needs assessment; values from standard pulse-oximetry guidance

low: Re-measure on a warm finger, sitting still.
Check the cabin's oxygen and carbon dioxide readings.
Ask a crewmate to measure theirs: if several are low, it is the air, not you.
Shortness of breath, blue lips or confusion with a low reading is urgent.
shift: Your oxygen level has dropped from your own normal. Check the cabin air readings.

indicators.name: Sleep last night
indicators.how: Enter the hours you actually slept, not the time in your sleep station. If you wear a tracker, use its number.
indicators.why: Crews in orbit see many sunrises a day and average about six hours of sleep. Short sleep degrades attention, mood, immunity and blood sugar within days.
sources: Adults need 7-9 hours (American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society consensus); NASA schedules 8.5 hours for crew sleep

low: Keep a fixed sleep and wake time, including rest days.
Dim the lights and screens for the last hour; use bright light in the first hour after waking.
No caffeine in the six hours before sleep.
Use earplugs and an eye mask, and check the airflow and temperature of your sleep station.
Avoid critical or hazardous tasks alone after a short night.
high: Long sleep can follow a sleep debt or signal illness or low mood. Check your temperature and mood entries.
shift: You are sleeping less than your own normal. Protect the next two nights before it builds into a debt.

indicators.name: Mood today
indicators.how: Pick the number that fits how you have felt overall today. There is no right answer; the point is the trend.
indicators.why: Isolation, confinement, workload and distance from home wear mood down gradually. People often notice it last in themselves, which is why it is logged.
sources: Self-rating on a 1-5 scale; no clinical cut-off, the trend against your own normal is what matters

low: Tell one crewmate how you are doing today.
Use your next private family or psychological conference; do not skip it.
Do your exercise session and get light exposure early in your day.
Take the scheduled rest time, and do one thing that is not work.
If your mood stays low for several days, talk to the crew medical officer. Thoughts of harming yourself are urgent.
shift: Your mood has been below your own normal. A few low days are expected; a sustained slide is worth acting on early.

indicators.name: Hydration (urine colour)
indicators.how: Compare the colour of your urine with the eight-step chart: 1 is nearly clear, 8 is brown. Use the first collection after waking.
indicators.why: The feeling of thirst is blunted in microgravity and fluid shifts hide dehydration. Concentrated urine also raises the risk of kidney stones, which is higher in flight.
sources: Eight-level urine colour chart (Armstrong et al.): 1-3 hydrated, 4-5 mildly dehydrated, 6-8 dehydrated

high: Drink 500 mL of water over the next hour, then steadily through the day.
Aim for pale straw colour by the afternoon.
Go easy on salty food and caffeine today.
Report flank pain, blood in the urine or pain passing urine: these suggest a kidney stone.
shift: Your urine is darker than your own normal. Raise your water intake today.

indicators.name: Exercise yesterday
indicators.how: Add up yesterday's resistance and aerobic exercise time, not counting set-up.
indicators.why: Exercise is the main defence against bone and muscle loss. Station crews are scheduled for about two hours a day, including loaded resistance work.
sources: NASA: station crews exercise about two hours per day; bone mineral density falls roughly 1-1.5% per month in weight-bearing bones without countermeasures

low: Book today's session now, resistance exercise first: loaded squats, deadlifts and heel raises protect the hip and spine.
If time is short, keep the resistance work and cut the aerobic part.
If you skipped because of pain, fatigue or equipment trouble, report which.
shift: You are exercising less than your own normal. Bone and muscle loss follow within weeks.

indicators.name: Body mass
indicators.how: Use the body-mass device at the same time of day, before eating. On a planetary surface, use the scale in the same clothing.
indicators.why: Unplanned loss of body mass means you are not eating enough or are losing muscle. A fall of 5% from your own baseline is clinically significant.
sources: Unintentional loss of 5% or more of body mass is treated as clinically significant in standard nutritional assessment

low: Log what you actually eat for three days and compare it with your planned intake.
Add an energy-dense snack between meals and do not skip meals for work.
Keep the resistance exercise going: under-eating plus unloading costs muscle fast.
high: Re-measure. A fast rise is usually fluid; check blood pressure and hydration.
shift: Your body mass has moved away from your baseline.

hazards.name: Space radiation
hazards.text: Outside Earth's magnetic shield the dose is many times higher. It raises long-term cancer risk and can affect the heart, the brain and the immune system.

hazards.name: Isolation and confinement
hazards.text: A small crew in a small space for months: sleep, mood and performance erode gradually.

hazards.name: Distance from Earth
hazards.text: No resupply, no evacuation, and a delay on every question to the ground. The crew has to spot and handle problems itself.

hazards.name: Gravity fields
hazards.text: Weightlessness, then partial gravity, then Earth again. Bone, muscle, the heart and fluid balance all adapt each time.

hazards.name: Hostile, closed environment
hazards.text: Recycled air and water, shared microbes, noise and constant artificial light.

environments.name: Space station, low Earth orbit
environments.delayNote: You can talk to the flight surgeons in real time.

environments.name: Deep-space transit to Mars
environments.delayNote: A question and its answer can take up to 44 minutes. Act on the guidance here first, then report.

environments.delayNote: Conversation with the ground is possible with a short lag.

environments.name: Surface rover, away from base
environments.delayNote: Help is hours away. Anything at the 'tell the medical officer' level means heading back.

equipment.name: Pulse oximeter
equipment.what: A fingertip clip that reads blood oxygen and pulse with light.

steps.t: Warm the hand you will use. Remove nail polish or anything covering the nail on that finger.
Anchor yourself and rest completely still. Start the timer and wait until it ends before you measure.
Open the clip and slide your index or middle finger in as far as it goes, nail facing the display side.
Rest the hand at chest height and keep it still. Do not talk. Let the numbers settle.
Read both numbers once they have been steady for ten seconds: SpO2 is your blood oxygen in %, PR or the heart symbol is your pulse in beats per minute.

space: Hold yourself with foot restraints, not with the hand being measured: a gripping hand gives a poor signal.
Hands are often cool in the cabin airflow. Warm the finger first; a cold finger reads low.
mistakes: Moving or talking during the reading
Cold fingers or nail polish
Strong light shining into the clip
Reading the number before it has settled
equipment.after: Wipe the inside of the clip with an alcohol wipe, let it dry, and stow it.

equipment.name: Blood pressure monitor
equipment.what: An automatic upper-arm cuff. It gives two numbers: upper (systolic) and lower (diastolic).
kit: Automatic monitor with an upper-arm cuff of the right size for your arm

steps.t: Before you start: no exercise, caffeine or large meal in the last 30 minutes, and use the toilet first.
Restrain yourself comfortably with your back supported. Start the timer and rest quietly until it ends.

Wrap the cuff on your bare upper arm, lower edge about two finger-widths above the elbow crease, with the tube or artery mark on the inside of the arm. It should be snug: two fingers fit under it, no more.
Support the arm so the cuff is level with your heart, palm up and relaxed.
Press Start. Stay still and silent until the cuff has fully deflated. Note the result.
Leave the cuff on, start the timer, and wait.
Take a second reading the same way. The second reading is the one you record.

space: Your arm floats. Rest it against your body or under a strap so the muscle is relaxed and the cuff stays at heart level.
Fluid shifts towards the head in the first days of flight can change your readings. That is why your own baseline matters more than a single number.
mistakes: Cuff over clothing, or the wrong cuff size
Talking, moving or tensing the arm
Arm above or below heart level
Measuring straight after exercise or caffeine
equipment.after: Squeeze the air out of the cuff, roll it loosely and stow it with the monitor.

equipment.name: Blood glucose meter
equipment.what: A hand-held meter that reads blood sugar from one drop of blood on a test strip.
kit: Lancing device with a new lancet

steps.t: Measure before breakfast, at least eight hours after you last ate or drank anything but water.
Clean the fingertip and dry it completely. Sugar, soap or alcohol left on the skin changes the result.
Insert a new test strip. The meter switches on and shows it is ready for blood.
Press the lancing device against the side of a fingertip, not the pad, and fire it.
Wipe away the first drop with gauze. Let a second round drop form without squeezing hard.
Touch the edge of the strip to the drop and hold it there until the meter beeps or starts counting down.
Read the result in mg/dL. Press gauze on the finger until it stops bleeding.

space: The drop does not fall: it clings to your finger as a bead. Bring the strip to the drop.
Keep the gauze in your other hand before you prick, so no blood drifts free in the cabin.
Cap and contain the used lancet at once. Nothing sharp may float.
mistakes: Wet or unwashed hands
Squeezing the finger hard, which dilutes the blood
A drop too small to fill the strip
Expired or damp strips
equipment.after: Put the lancet in the sharps container and the strip and gauze in the biohazard waste. Wipe the meter.

equipment.name: Ear thermometer
equipment.what: An infrared thermometer that reads body temperature from the eardrum in about two seconds.

steps.t: Wait 30 minutes after exercise, a hot or cold drink, or wearing a headset over that ear.
Fit a new probe cover until it clicks.
With your free hand, pull the top of the ear gently up and back to straighten the ear canal.
Insert the probe snugly so it seals the canal, pointing towards the opposite temple.
Press the button and hold still until it beeps. Read the temperature in °C.

space: Use the same ear every time. The two ears can differ by a few tenths of a degree, and it is the change from your own normal that counts.
Body temperature runs slightly higher in flight, because heat does not rise off the skin without gravity. Compare with your own in-flight readings.
mistakes: A loose fit that lets cabin air in
Switching between ears
Earwax blocking the canal
Measuring straight after exercise
equipment.after: Eject the probe cover into the waste and stow the thermometer in its case.

equipment.name: Urine colour chart
equipment.what: An eight-step colour scale, from 1 (nearly clear) to 8 (brown), that shows how well hydrated you are.
kit: Clear urine collection bag or container

steps.t: Use your first collection after waking: it is the most concentrated of the day and the most comparable from day to day.
Collect a sample in the clear bag or container.
Hold it next to the chart under white light, against a white background.
Pick the step that matches most closely. Between two steps, choose the darker one.
Record the number, from 1 to 8.

space: You feel less thirsty in weightlessness even when you need water, so do not wait for thirst.
Dehydration and bone loss together raise the risk of kidney stones. Staying at 1 to 3 on the chart is one of the simplest protections.
mistakes: Judging the colour under coloured or dim light
Using a later sample on some days and the first on others
Forgetting that B vitamins turn urine bright yellow and beetroot turns it pink: note it and judge by darkness, not hue
equipment.after: Dispose of the sample through the waste system as usual and clean your hands.

equipment.name: Body mass measurement device
equipment.what: In weightlessness a scale reads nothing. This device pushes or pulls you with a known force and works out your mass from how fast you accelerate.
kit: Its calibration mass, if your procedure calls for one

steps.t: Measure at the same point in your day each time, before eating and after using the toilet, in light clothing with empty pockets.
Unstow and lock the device in place. Run its zero or calibration check as its own procedure describes.
Mount it: wrap your legs around the support, rest your chin or chest on the pad, and grip the handles.
Make your whole body rigid, hold your breath, and release the mechanism. Stay rigid until the movement stops.
Repeat for the number of runs the device asks for, usually three to five. It averages them.
Read the averaged body mass in kg.

space: Any loose movement, including breathing, adds error. Stiff and still is what makes the reading repeatable.
On the Moon or Mars use the surface scale set to show mass. A normal scale there would show a fraction of your Earth weight.
mistakes: A relaxed or shifting posture
Different clothing or pocket contents from one week to the next
Measuring after a meal one week and before it the next
equipment.after: Lock the mechanism, wipe the pads and stow the device.

equipment.name: Wrist sleep tracker
equipment.what: A watch-like motion sensor worn on the wrist. It works out when you were asleep from how much you moved.

steps.t: Wear the tracker on your non-dominant wrist, snug enough that it does not slide.
When you settle to sleep, press its event button, or note the time.
Keep it on all night. On waking, press the event button again.
Sync the tracker and read last night's total sleep time, not the time spent in your sleep station.
No tracker? Estimate: lights-out to wake-up, minus the time it took to fall asleep and any time awake in the night.

space: Your arms float while you sleep, so the tracker sees more movement than on Earth and can under-count. Compare with your own in-flight nights.
There is no natural night. Keep lights-out and wake-up at fixed times so your readings mean the same thing each day.
mistakes: Entering time in the sleep station instead of time asleep
Taking the tracker off to charge at night
Forgetting naps: add them only if your procedure says so
equipment.after: Charge the tracker during a waking period so it is ready for the night.

equipment.name: Resistance exercise device
equipment.what: A machine that provides load without weight, so squats, deadlifts and heel raises can stress your bones and muscles as they would on Earth.

steps.t: Inspect the device before loading it: cables, bar or handles, and foot plate. Do not use it if anything looks worn or loose; report it.
Warm up for five to ten minutes with light aerobic exercise or unloaded movements.
Set the load from your session plan. If you have missed sessions, start lower than last time.
Take your position: feet flat on the plate, bar or harness seated on the shoulders, back straight.
Do each set under control: about two seconds down, two seconds up, no bouncing. Stop if you feel sharp pain.
Rest between sets.
When you finish, add up the minutes of resistance and aerobic exercise, not counting set-up. That total is what you record tomorrow as “exercise yesterday”.

space: Squats, deadlifts and heel raises load the hip and spine, where bone is lost fastest. If time is short, keep these and drop the rest.
Sweat does not drip, it pools on the skin. Towel off during rests so it does not float free.
mistakes: Skipping the inspection
Raising the load too fast after a break
Fast, bouncing repetitions
Counting set-up and rest as exercise time
equipment.after: Return the load to zero, wipe down the contact surfaces and stow the bar or harness.

equipmentNote: These are general instructions for standard devices. Where your mission's own procedure for the hardware on board says something different, follow the procedure.
